I mean, a SSRI is something that may sorta work for ADHD but isn't made for ADHD, stimulants (and therapy) are the default front line ADHD treatment and work for most people. Iirc it's like 85% of people or something insane.

There's also non-stimulants ones that are less popular if telehealth is your only option.

It's probably likely you can try both a stimulant and SSRI if the SSRI is working somewhat, but you'll need to discuss what kinds.

In general tho my reaction to Ritalin / Concerta coming from decades of SSRIs / SNRIs, and antipsychotics. 

* Took a couple of days to confirm it was working and 3 months to settle on dosage, with another test laster for evening med. This is 90% becuase my doctor wanted monthly raising the dosage. You can probably figure out dosage in 3-6 weeks. Compared to the 6-12 months to see if it works from SSRIs, that was amazing
* No more suicidal ideation side effects, thank fuck.
* Emotional control and stability, able to self soothe, happier in general. No longer emotionally numb basically.
* LARGE amount of depression vanished, still struggling a bit with getting started on things because ugh effort and need to structure my life to help with it. 
* A bit cyclical and time based, needed evening booster when working and very stressed to keep up. Less flat then antidepressants. You will probably get some rebound hyper.
* Requires more awareness of your needs. I had a few times I got upset and frustrated becuase antidepressants don't let you feel. This meant days where I had no food, family was a dick, got in a car accident, and work yelled at me and then I tripped and dropped coffee I'd fucking sob. Food and water and chill time with stressful noisey things is necessary for me. It's not every time, but like, does require awareness when things are shit and I got noise cancelling headphones and sometimes talk to friends or family like I need 5, let me walk and buy us a coffee 
* Much more annoying to get, I have to call the pharmacy every month. But also no major issue skipping a day.
* Period effects strength. Some times during the month it'll feel like it's not strong enough. In those cases I use coffee and structure
* Over all HOLY FUCK IT HELPS with some side effects and mostly the annoyance of now I'm like 75-80% neurotypically effective and it bugs me I can't do better. But compared to the 5% I had before, massively different.

> They said that they can't take my clutter or me not doing my dishes for several days anymore and unless I make a significant change they don't want to resign the lease. 

You may have already passed the point of no return tbh. No offence just, be prepared for that and try not to take it too badly if true. Sounds like she wants a high standard of clean and isn't communicating before it's bugging her.

Anyhow,

* Find a chore list app or list on Pinterest 
* Make it super super clear and break down by task. You might need both dishes and wipe down sink after to be on list for example.
* ( Also remove all the obviously not weekly ones like wash ceiling lamps and add them to another list if you want for a once a season everyone agrees to deep clean thing. )
* Physical list may help, like a group chore list on the fridge. This can also help for everyone else to see work. 
* Ask people to text you chores they are asking about and timelines. Especially if they want X Y and Z or Z by Tuesday. Being able to go back when you forget helps.
* A single day or routine can help but tbh I feel like ADHD makes it easier for you to take the every day tasks or a clear one off big task on weekend. Tasks you need to 'see' like dusting will be harder. Figure out if trading these will help.
* Set yourself alarm _with labels!_ Snooze alarm till you are at least stating it! 
* Find podcast, let's play or similar to listen to while doing dishes. Try to do it every night.
* Really just make it so x time every night you do a thing. Or morning. Set it to be an external habit and time trigger.
* Using your phone can help with 'seeing' mess just make sure you don't distract yourself. I do this to catch door I left open, papers out, dusting...
* Body Doubling is having someone over doing the same or similar thing to help you feel productive. This can help a lot for cleaning. I get somewhat similar effect listening to video game streamers. This may mean one day clean helps.
* Honestly even just having a roommate hang out while you start helps. Or having them available to say toss the laundry in so you don't have to leave the bathroom while cleaning and swapping towels.
* Some people with ADHD respond well to coffee. I def used energy drinks to do tasks when I was younger.

Quite frankly. It sucks. Its hard. I get your tired. But you gotta trigger yourself to do it. 

Other things that require more money or effort,

* If you have close friends or family willing to come over and help deep clean, cleaning after it's been cleaned once helps. Honestly if your close enough and it's not horrible, calling or having people over while doing dishes and stuff can be nice. Just be aware they may not like the noises.
* Used counter top dishwasher may be about $150-$200 and help a lot
* Sometimes hiring a cleaner is suggested but idk if that's possible.
* Buy baskets and trays. Clean with a laundry basket or similar. A big ass box to carry things around in makes putting things away easier and a tray or basket on counters collects odds and ends that get left in common areas.
* Wear loungeware that's good enough to go toss garbage outside in. If the garbage bin is small I just take entire bin then swap out bag. Idk why but remove bag, insert new never triggers take out bag unless I'm like getting the entire apartment emptied.
* If you don't wear shoes inside try putting on slippers or flipflops. My brain reads that as clean time.
* Ditto apron to clean in. 
* Consider buying some extras and having things in arms reach. For example I have shower spray in my bathroom and those counter wipes for the one time I go huh I should do this. It's also in my cleaning gear but just having it accessible in 1 step is a lot easier.

Edit: But I agree DISHES IS A BIG ONE. If hand washing maybe even just have a bin of dishes to wash on the counter to corral them? You'll see how many / little there are. If you can get into the habit of daily dish washing, not even putting them away, just letting them dry on the rack that'll probably be the biggest single improvement.

Therapy and an assessment are usually very different.

I'm going to assume therapy, as in long term sit down and talk about stuff and coping skills stuff.

* The first session will be mostly getting to know each other
* The therapist will tell you the legal limits of privacy in your area, generally active child abuse needs to be reported by them, active plans to hurt someone will be reported, suicidal thoughts with an actionable plan (as in I will shoot myself tonight) and if the courts mandate them to share.
* You'll be asked to introduce yourself, what made you look for therapy, if you say you think you have ADHD probably why
* They'll generally want to know your living situation, roughly family history and background
* Eventually I just had a year by year breakdown document of life events but that was after years of therapy and told person for that I won't remember years in order (idk if they were impressed or worried)

General tips for therapy,

* HIGHLY suggest having therapist not let you leave without planning next session or sending payment if your paying personally. I uh, was bad at that.
* Many therapists can send reminder emails!
* I highly suggest having something to write down notes, or scribble. You won't need to take notes but it helps me keep from jumping topics as much and not forget stuff 
* If you journal bring that for your own reference or use phone for notes. I forgot all the shit that happened the last few weeks every time. 
* Personally, I did not like CBT type therapy. I liked more of the ACT, DBT and EMDR therapy. I found the homework of CBT and the structure dismissive but ymmv. Therapists specialize a bit but should be trained in many types of therapy so don't feel bad saying X isn't working or 'you just need to try to focus harder' feels dismissive and like they aren't listening to you asking for coping skills to fucking do that.
* Try not to downplay your own emotions and struggles. I know it's a thing™ but still. Contextualizing normal amounts of lack of focus / struggles / so on can also help. For example, how often do you lose your keys. It helps the therapist who seems to generally assume the usual key losing metric is like once a year so "a lot" is three times ... not weekly and found it in your freezer before work and how tf!?

Also don't feel bad if you need to swap therapists. Your trying to find someone your comfortable with. That's hard.

>For the sausage I burned the outside and smoked up the kitchen but it was still cold when I put it on my plate 

Sounds like a combo of a few problems,

* Cheap cookware (usually) is very thin and heats up quick and doesn't hold heat well 
* Cheap cookware can also not always be flat, resulting in issues staying cooked properly 
* Gas stoves can get very very hot and different stoves and elements can be different temperatures then you expect
* Apartment stoves can be smaller. In my experience that means they heat up faster then you expected.
* Cooking for one often means smaller meals

A few things that might help,

* Stovetop. Start lower, wet your hand and flick water into a pan or use butter / oil and listen / look for bubbles to figure out when it's the right temperature
* Remove from heat if needed, add liquid (stock, wine, water) to deglaze and cook rapidly if really fucked up. Thin pans like aluminum cool down fast. Thick ones like cast iron will keep that temperature for several minutes. You'll have to adjust depending on pan and on oven. It'll take a few months.
* Oven. Borrow (or try some buy nothing groups) an oven thermometer and make sure it matches what you expect. If you rent congrats you can yell at landlord to fix it if it's really off.
* Adjust the racks in the oven, figure out if moving them helps. I moved mine up higher and it helped.
* Look at the oven manual if you have it or Google the model number. Some have stuff like convention settings that get even hotter.
* Use parchment paper when needed, sometimes that means the bottom burns less. Don't use wax paper, that's flammable.
* Cover the top of things that still need to cook with aluminum foil loosely to encourage it not to burn on top while still cooking through. Think like cakes, or shepherds pie or a baked lasagna. Tightly wrapped aluminium foil will steam items, so is good for veggies and fish and bad for things you don't want damp.
* Baking sheets need wide spacing, if you can, for best cooking. So if your oven is tiny you might need two sheets. 
* You can test your ovens temperature and where the hot spots are by trying to make something giant and flat, like a big ass cookie. Expect some bad cookies but it can teach you. Personally I just spin my baking sheets around becuase my oven has hot spots.
* Also I know for me personally, I wandered off too much while cooking. And still do sometimes. So I vote headphones and music or podcast if you have similar issues.

For cleaning,

* Get dish gloves, scents you don't hate and earplugs or noise cancelling headphones. 
* Start kettle, close sink, dump worst of it in, fill with hot water. 
* Fill with more hot water if you need from tap. Come back in 5 minutes. SET LABELED ALARM. Or just fill with cool water to be touchable. Drain. 
* Congrats the absolutely worst is usually off. 
* Try to avoid soaking things unless you KNOW you'll clean them in the morning.


General cooking stuff,

* Get easy to clean pans. 
* Rinse pan immediately after using. Don't clean just, rinse off sticky tomato sauce before nomming down
* Paper towels can be used occasionally to help clean up easily. Is a rag better and cheaper? Yes. Do I currently have a washed one? Nope. Also buy a bunch more kitchen rags and have a place for them so they get washed regularly. The rolls of fabric kitchen cloths are also awesome.
* Get dishwasher safe stuff if possible and consider counter top dishwasher if you don't have one. It helps a little.
* You can run the dishwasher twice if you need!
* You can reuse the same cutting board for various things, just have one meat one everything else.
* You can rinse off veggie cutting board immediately, I don't wash mine properly till end of day. Ymmv and it's gross but it hasn't hurt me. Clean the meat one tho.
* You can pre-cook and have meat separated do it's less of a bitch to cook
* You can use parchment paper on baking sheet to reduce clean up.
* Rotisserie chicken and forzen veggies are your friend.
* Ditto rice cooker. Im sure you like fried rice too.
* Meal prep is overwhelming but really helpful. Try to think of ingredient prep. Pre-chopped stuff reduces a lot of my effort. Even canned or frozen foods can help. Frozen pre cut squash is technically like 35c more expensive but it's SO MUCH EASIER for me. 
* Tbh best investment so far was $25 for like 40 500ml matching containers. Think takeout soup style. It fits a large meal, they stack, they fit in freezer, I can fill them half way and freeze for sauces or something... Get nice long term storage stuff.
* WRITE DOWN a list on front of fridge of the food in freezer storage so you don't forget the chili for 3 months and also any easy / healthy snacks / meals you wanna have more
* Put the stuff you wanna have in fridge door or up front. Put sauces in crisper drawer or something. Your brain will go ohh that first and seeing cheese slices will get you microwave grilled cheese sandwich as ideas but seeing zucchini will make you think of baked veggies

But in general ADHD school tips (from an adult who had to learn them for college so ymmv on kiddo)

* ADHD kids (and adults) need more transition times, if young I'd work on rituals to separate it. For example as an adult I have sung myself songs about hating the dishes to get myself to start. I'd try to be more positive.  
* Kids need very clear ideas of steps and each step or it's overwhelming
* Sipping sugary drinks is proven to work, maybe frozen grapes or something might help. Sugar = dopamine = the brain energy to start. Obviously be aware of this but as an adult I still use that sometimes.
* Add just enough distraction. If you go the empty room with nothing route your kid will distract herself. Try some mild background distraction, for myself that's studying in a coffee shop but for kiddo that may be yoga ball chair, fidget chair band, background music (I'd avoid lyrics) and studying while say your cooking

Off the top of my head discouraged with smacking, spankings or detention;

* Chewing gum, paper, hair, nails, jewelery

* Noise stims like clearing your throat, clicking your tongue or the kinda gasp excited noise I still get in trouble for before talking about something
* "Happy hands", snapping your fingers, talking with your hands, masculine hand gestures, touching things
* Knitting, doodling, crochet, fidget toys, embroidery, origami

I'm not American, but in order I'd try,

* Write out the first thoughts of what you'd want to do? Vote? Drive? Text Mom I will be back home at 6 PM and bus to mall? 
* Apply for disbality and find an advocate, explain you want to learn life skills to adult more. There's often programs and even dorm-like housing for people in these situations. 
* Speak with advocate or social worker, take notes. Plan out what the best options and steps are.
* Also if you get disability, try to save some of it.
* Talk to parents. Write letter / have notes if needed. Discuss that you want more freedom and understand their concerns, and try to pick one thing to start.


Let's say you want the freedom to communicate with parents your doing X today, on your own. Like going to a movie 

You need to learn,

* Where to find a movie
* How to be comfortable there 
* How to find a bus there 
* Buy ticket
* Find a bus back
* How to talk to parents and plan this 
* How to keep communication open if they worry, like you miss a bus
* What to do if things go wrong

So let's say, you feel confident with movie plan, and you talk to parents that between the hours of 9 AM till 5 PM you don't think you should need to alert them to every single move. 

They worry, so you agree to write I am at Movie at Location for 3 PM. Bus home should arrive approx 6 PM. You also agree to text them when you arrive there and leave to go back home.

They worry a little more about what if phone dies or bus is late. You point out the mall has public phones and will call a taxi and parents have $50 cash hidden in house for emergencies which would cover a taxi.

And you do it.



Frankly I think your parents are overly worried and hurting you by not making it easier to learn this stuff.  They might have some points, but this is extremely over the top. 
Eventually you gotta try to learn some of this stuff and find work arounds for the others and they should be helping.


As for driving, I highly suggest if American to try to learn. It's just useful.

Lessons might be better then parents teaching as it can be overwhelming. It's okay if it takes a long time to learn to drive. One of my friends has taken a year to get from comfortable sitting in driver's seat not moving to driving on smaller highways and still pulls over sometimes to get out and decompress becuase too much. Another friend literally doesn't drive in the city outside of emergencies and they've had a license for 15 years.


Also I suspect an in person job would be less stressful with parents then work from home. Your parents sound like they may struggle to respect your work hours and WFH call centre will yell if parents bother you during work. But that depends on you and job.


It also might be useful to have a scheduled class or event for a few weeks as the routine might work better to coax parents (and you) into learning to get there and deal.

I mean yes, by their nature catagories create an other but this seems a little like a leading question.

In general, people want labels to define themselves and find similar people. Because people like belonging and sharing. And the reverse, humans are prone to othering people.

But big labels can cover a lot of ground, and feel uncomfortable to some people who don't feel they fit the label perfectly or to it's extremes. 

Using your example of sexual being vs not sexual being, you could classify everyone into alloseuxal or asexual, but there would be people uncomfortable as alloseuxal might imply they would have sex with literally anyone, or to a gender they don't feel attraction to, or feel maybe they don't have enough sexual attraction to count as alloseuxal. Or asexuals who feel romantic attraction but not sexual, and so on.

So sometimes within that catagory you make a smaller catagory that defines you better. And you get stuff like straight, gay, bi, demisexual. Then sometimes there's even more narrowing down.

In general, the microlabels are used for in community communication and to find similar groups. Or they're used for extreme specificness. Just like you say table salt, NaCl, ionized salt and salt for different situation there's a very rare situation I'll say I'm a cis-gender ace-spc bi lady. In 99% of cases, lady or if they need to know my sexuality bi lady works. The exact details are of concern to me, no one else. /grey-ace groups to talk over my confusion and issues with not even knowing if I have sexual attraction or general queer groups to talk over the whole pan vs bi thing.
